extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics; poets and critics interested in classical theory of epic and tragic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating epic and tragic poetry, covering diction (metaphor, rare words, compounds), plot/structure (single action, beginning/middle/end), metre, the use of the wonderful/irrational, and standards for poetic correctness. Draws on Aristotle's Poetics with editorial notes and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced infusion of rare words and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain infusion of strange (or rare) words, the metaphorical, the ornamental, and other such elements is necessary to style; they will raise it above the commonplace and mean, while the use of proper words will make it perspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not compose a style wholly of strange words (that becomes a jargon) nor wholly of metaphors (that becomes a riddle). Combine rare/ornamental elements with proper/current words to achieve distinction without obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate use of licenses of speech (lengthening/contraction/alteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthening, contraction, and alteration of words contribute to a clearness of diction that is remote from commonness; by deviating in exceptional cases from the normal idiom the language gains distinction while partial conformity gives perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics err in censuring these licenses; employ them sparingly for distinction but avoid constant deviation which harms clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obtrusive or grotesque diction
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ such license at all obtrusively is, no doubt, grotesque; metaphors and strange words used without propriety, with the express purpose of being ludicrous, have the same effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphor and rare words with propriety and moderation; if used to be ludicrous they damage the style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-choice can determine beauty vs triviality
rubrics_metrics.description: The alteration of a single word (e.g., a rarer term instead of the ordinary one) can make one verse appear beautiful and another trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful selection between common and rare terms materially affects the reader's aesthetic judgment; test substitutions to judge effect (examples: Aeschylus vs Euripides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate word-types by metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic. In heroic poetry all these varieties are serviceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match lexical choices to the meter/genre: heroic verse tolerates rare words and metaphors; dithyrambs suit compounds; iambic favors metaphor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iambic diction should reproduce familiar speech
rubrics_metrics.description: In iambic verse, which reproduces, as far as may be, familiar speech, the most appropriate words are those which are found even in prose: the current or proper, the metaphorical, the ornamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer words common to prose in iambic contexts to preserve naturalness and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-action requirement for narrative imitation (epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: As to poetic imitation narrative in form and employing a single metre, the plot manifestly ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles: it should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to make an epic cover an entire vast subject at once; detach a single portion and admit episodes as subordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish epic from historical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic differs from historical compositions which present a single period and many loosely connected events; epic should present a single action producing a coherent result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid merely chronicling contemporaneous events that do not tend to one result; aim for unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic must include structural elements of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must have as many kinds as Tragedy: it must be simple, or complex, or 'ethical,' or 'pathetic.' The parts also, with the exception of song and scenery, are the same; it requires Reversals of Intention, Recognitions, and Tragic Incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure epic contains necessary plot mechanisms (recognition, reversal, tragic incident) and artistic thought and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate scale for epic (single view)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; this condition will be satisfied by poems on a smaller scale than the old epics, answering in length to the group of tragedies presented at a single sitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the thematic scope so the poem can be comprehended as a coherent whole; epic has capacity to enlarge but should still be graspable as one view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic's advantage: simultaneous events and episodic variety
rubrics_metrics.description: In Epic poetry, owing to the narrative form, many events simultaneously transacted can be presented; these, if relevant to the subject, add mass and dignity and relieve the story with varying episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple simultaneous events and episodes to enrich and vary the narrative, while avoiding sameness that produces satiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic metre suitability and prohibition on mixing metres
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all measures the heroic is the stateliest and the most massive; hence it most readily admits rare words and metaphors. It would be absurd to mix different metres, as Chaeremon did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer heroic metre for large-scale narrative and avoid mixing metres in a single poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person, for it is not this that makes him an imitator; Homer brings in personages directly, each with characteristic qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the characters' speech and action carry the imitation; avoid excessive authorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit the wonderful appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: The wonderful is admitted in Tragedy; it has wider scope in Epic because the person acting is not seen; the poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ the wonderful when it pleases; prefer incidents that maintain a degree of probability or plausibility to maintain audience acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrational parts in tragic plots
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts. Everything irrational should, if possible, be excluded; or at all events it should lie outside the action of the play (as in Oedipus' ignorance), not within the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce absurd incidents within the drama's action; if irrational is necessary, make it external or vest it with an air of likelihood so the audience accepts it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction elaborated in pauses; avoid over-brilliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. Conversely, character and thought are merely obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate diction for moments of pause; during active characterization and thought, favor clear, character-revealing speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of imitation object (threefold)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet being an imitator must imitate one of three objects—things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which mode of imitation (actual, reputed, ideal) underlies the poem and maintain consistency with that choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate vehicle of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The vehicle of expression is language—either current terms or, it may be, rare words or metaphors. There are also many modifications of language which we concede to the poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select among current terms, rare words, and metaphors according to the poem's aims and mode; recognize that standards of correctness differ between poetry and other arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish essential versus accidental faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the art of poetry there are two kinds of faults—those which touch its essence, and those which are accidental. If a poet has imitated incorrectly through want of capacity, the error is inherent; if the failure is due to a wrong choice (technical inaccuracies), the error is not essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing, distinguish between failures of poetic capacity (essential) and incidental errors or bad choices; avoid tolerating essential faults and correct accidental ones where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors may be justified if they achieve the art's end
rubrics_metrics.description: If the poet describes the impossible, he is guilty of an error; but the error may be justified if the end of the art is thereby attained—if the effect of this part of the poem is thus rendered more striking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow deviations from strict truth only when they serve the poem's artistic purpose better than strict adherence to truth would.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual evaluation of sayings/actions
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining whether what has been said or done by someone is poetically right, we must consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, in whose interest, or for what end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lines or actions in their dramatic context (speaker, audience, timing, motive) rather than in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use linguistic usage and dialectal senses to resolve difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Other difficulties may be resolved by due regard to the usage of language; a rare word may be employed in a non-literal or regional sense (e.g., words used differently by Cretans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to dialectical, colloquial, or non-literal meanings when interpreting or employing rare words; this can justify apparently odd usages.
